title: The honored guest
hook: Dhanna's rock; a shelf of five things for God
carry: the murti is an honored guest

segments.voice: Yesterday, the meru, and your first full round. Your line was the mala: one full round of 108. This week, the practice gets a home. Literally.

In many Hindu homes there's a small shrine. In a big house it might be a whole room; in a student apartment, a shelf above the desk. In a lot of kitchens it's a little alcove near the stove, with a picture of Krishna leaning against the spice jars and a lamp lit every morning for as long as anyone remembers. It's called the mandir, the temple, or the puja room, even when it's only a shelf. And a simple one can come down to five things.
screen: `A ROOM, OR A SHELF.` → `KRISHNA BY THE SPICE JARS.` → `IT COMES DOWN TO FIVE THINGS.`

segments.voice: Who lives on that shelf? Dhanna was a farm boy in Rajasthan, and the story told of him goes like this. He watched a brahmin worship a sacred stone every morning, and begged for one of his own. To get rid of him, the brahmin handed him an ordinary rock. Dhanna took it home, set it in a clean place, and at mealtime put his own food in front of it and waited for God to eat. God didn't. So Dhanna didn't either. Days went by, the boy hungry, stubborn and sure. And in the story, God came and ate from his plate. A plain rock, offered to with that much love, had become a home for God. Here's the teaching. Many Hindus understand a murti, the image on the shrine, as a place where the divine is truly present, and welcome it as an honored guest; others see it as a focus for the mind; both are held. That's why the five simple things are what a good host offers. One, the image itself, the guest. Two, a lamp, for light. Three, a flower, something beautiful, given away. Four, a bell, rung to begin, to call the attention of the divine, many say, and your own. Five, water, the first thing you'd offer anyone who walks in. Nothing costly; Dhanna's rock cost nothing. Keep it clean and a little apart, and remember: a shelf you pass every morning beats a perfect room you never enter. The murti is an honored guest.
screen: `DHANNA'S ORDINARY ROCK.` · `HE WOULDN'T EAT UNTIL GOD DID.` · `THE MURTI — AN HONORED GUEST.` · `IMAGE, LAMP, FLOWER, BELL, WATER.` · then, large: `THE MURTI IS AN HONORED GUEST.`

segments.voice: Choose a place, a shelf, the corner of a dresser, a windowsill, and clear it. Gather what you have: an image or a picture that means something to you, a candle or tea light, a flower or a leaf from outside, anything that rings, even a spoon on a glass, and a small cup of water, and set them down slowly. If you can't do it right now, picture exactly where it will go, then sit in front of it and breathe.
Five objects. An image, a lamp, a flower, a bell, and water: what a good host sets out for the guest on a home shrine.
Take this with you: the murti is an honored guest. Dhanna's rock was enough, and a shelf is plenty. One hundred eleven days in.

howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep a small shrine, from a whole puja room to a kitchen shelf, with an image or picture of the family's deities, a lamp, flowers, a bell and water, where daily puja is offered.

what a scholar hears: Dhanna, a devotee remembered in Nabhadas's Bhaktamal and its commentaries, with hymns attributed to him in the Guru Granth Sahib; the murti understood by many as a place of presence after consecration (prana pratishtha); the upacharas, puja's offerings of hospitality, of which these five are a simple home set, not the classical list.
